items.prompt: What is the main chemical that makes up the bulk of Jupiter and Saturn?

options.label: Hydrogen
options.feedback: Correct. Hydrogen is the most abundant element in Jupiter and Saturn, making up most of their mass.

options.label: Helium
options.feedback: Helium is present, but it is the second most abundant element. Hydrogen dominates the composition.

options.label: Methane
options.feedback: Methane is found in the atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, not as the bulk of Jupiter or Saturn.

options.label: Ammonia
options.feedback: Ammonia exists as a trace gas and in clouds, but it is not the main component of these planets.

items.ok_line: Hydrogen is the primary gas in Jupiter and Saturn.
items.ko_line: Remember that hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
items.exp_text: Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of hydrogen, with helium as the second major component. This hydrogen exists in gas form at the surface, but deeper inside, pressure squeezes it into a liquid metallic state. The small amounts of methane and ammonia present are responsible for some cloud colors, but they are not the bulk of the planet.

items.prompt: Where does the Great Red Spot of Jupiter actually sit?

options.label: On the solid surface of the planet
options.feedback: Jupiter has no solid surface; the Great Red Spot is a storm in the atmosphere, not on any ground.

options.label: In the deep interior below the clouds
options.feedback: The storm is visible from the outside, located in the upper cloud layers, not hidden deep inside.

options.label: In the upper cloud layer of the atmosphere
options.feedback: Correct. The Great Red Spot is a swirling storm in Jupiter's upper cloud deck, visible as an oval feature.

options.label: Between the planet and its innermost moon
options.feedback: That region is space, not part of the planet. The spot is an atmospheric feature on Jupiter itself.

items.ok_line: The Great Red Spot is a storm in Jupiter's clouds.
items.ko_line: The spot is not on the surface, but in the atmosphere.
items.exp_title: Location of the Great Red Spot
items.exp_text: The Great Red Spot is a giant, high-pressure storm that has been observed for centuries. It sits in Jupiter's upper cloud layer, spinning counterclockwise. There is no solid surface beneath it—the storm is part of the planet's thick atmosphere, which extends down to the metallic hydrogen layer.

items.prompt: What are Saturn's rings primarily made of?

options.label: Dust and fine sand
options.feedback: Dust is present, but the rings are mostly made of larger chunks of ice, not just fine particles.

options.label: Chunks of water ice
options.feedback: Correct. Saturn's rings are composed of countless pieces of water ice, ranging from tiny grains to house-sized boulders.

options.label: Solid rock and metal
options.feedback: Rock and metal are rare in the rings; they would be too dense and dark. Ice dominates.

options.label: Liquid water
options.feedback: The rings are solid icy particles, not a liquid. They orbit individually around Saturn.

items.ok_line: Saturn's rings are made of water ice chunks.
items.ko_line: Rings are icy, not rocky or liquid.
items.exp_text: Saturn's rings are vast collections of icy particles, each on its own orbit around the planet. The ice reflects sunlight well, which makes the rings shine brightly. Some particles are as small as dust, while others are as large as a small car. There is very little rocky material, and the rings are not solid sheets but a swarm of individual pieces.

items.prompt: Which of these planets has the most tilted spin axis, lying almost on its side?

options.label: Jupiter
options.feedback: Jupiter's axis tilt is only about 3 degrees, so it spins nearly upright, not on its side.

options.label: Saturn
options.feedback: Saturn's tilt is about 27 degrees, noticeable but not enough to lie on its side.

options.label: Neptune
options.feedback: Neptune's tilt is about 28 degrees, similar to Saturn's, but not extreme like Uranus.

options.label: Uranus
options.feedback: Correct. Uranus has an axial tilt of about 98 degrees, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side.

items.ok_line: Uranus spins on its side, almost in the plane of its orbit.
items.ko_line: Remember that only Uranus is tilted that dramatically.
items.exp_text: Uranus rotates with its axis nearly horizontal, tilted about 98 degrees relative to its orbital plane. This means its poles face the Sun directly during parts of its year, and its equator is nearly vertical. This unusual orientation is thought to result from a massive collision early in its history.

items.prompt: Why do Jupiter and Saturn appear yellow-brown to our eyes?

options.label: They have clouds of ammonia and other compounds that scatter light
options.feedback: Correct. The upper clouds contain ammonia ice and various sulfur compounds, which give these planets their tan and brown hues.

options.label: Their surfaces are made of rusty rock
options.feedback: They have no solid surface; the color comes from clouds, not from rock.

options.label: They reflect the yellow light of the Sun
options.feedback: All planets reflect sunlight; the color depends on what the clouds are made of, not the Sun's color.

options.label: They are mostly made of methane gas
options.feedback: Methane gives Uranus and Neptune their blue color, but Jupiter and Saturn have little methane in their visible clouds.

items.ok_line: Ammonia clouds and impurities make them yellow-brown.
items.ko_line: Color comes from atmospheric composition, not surface.
items.exp_title: Why Jupiter and Saturn are yellow-brown
items.exp_text: Jupiter and Saturn have thick atmospheres with clouds of ammonia crystals and other compounds like ammonium hydrosulfide. These particles absorb some wavelengths and reflect others, producing shades of yellow, brown, and cream. The exact colors vary with altitude and temperature, but the overall effect is distinctly warm-toned, unlike the cooler blue of methane-rich planets.

items.prompt: Inside Jupiter, what form does hydrogen take deep below the visible clouds?

options.label: It stays as a normal gas all the way down
options.feedback: At great depth, the pressure is so high that hydrogen stops being a normal gas and turns into a different state.

options.label: It becomes a solid ice
options.feedback: Hydrogen does not freeze into ice; instead, under extreme pressure it becomes a liquid metal.

options.label: It becomes a liquid metal
options.feedback: Correct. The immense pressure inside Jupiter squeezes hydrogen into a liquid metallic state, which conducts electricity.

options.label: It turns into helium liquid
options.feedback: Helium is a separate element; it does not change hydrogen. The question asks about hydrogen itself.

items.ok_line: Deep inside Jupiter, hydrogen is a liquid metal.
items.ko_line: The deep interior is liquid metallic hydrogen, not gas.
items.exp_text: Beneath Jupiter's cloud layers, pressure and temperature rise dramatically. At about a quarter of the way to the center, the pressure forces hydrogen's electrons to detach, turning it into a liquid that conducts electricity like a metal. This layer is the reason Jupiter has such a strong magnetic field—the moving metallic hydrogen generates it.

items.prompt: Which planet has the most extreme winds, with speeds exceeding 2,000 kilometers per hour?

options.label: Jupiter
options.feedback: Jupiter's winds are fast, but they peak around 600 km/h, well below the record on another planet.

options.label: Neptune
options.feedback: Correct. Neptune has the strongest sustained winds of any planet in the solar system, reaching over 2,000 km/h.

options.label: Saturn
options.feedback: Saturn's winds can be strong, but they are slower than Neptune's, typically around 1,800 km/h at most.

options.label: Uranus
options.feedback: Uranus has moderate winds, generally below 900 km/h, much weaker than Neptune's.

items.ok_line: Neptune's winds are the fastest in the solar system.
items.ko_line: The fastest winds are on Neptune, not the others.
items.exp_text: Despite being the farthest from the Sun and receiving little energy, Neptune has incredibly violent winds. They blow mostly in an east-west direction and can reach speeds over 2,000 km/h. The reason is unclear, but it likely relates to Neptune's internal heat source and its fast rotation, which stirs the atmosphere powerfully.

items.prompt: What color do Uranus and Neptune appear, due to methane in their atmospheres?

options.label: Blue-green
options.feedback: Correct. Methane absorbs red light and reflects blue-green light, giving both planets their distinctive hue.

options.label: Yellow-brown
options.feedback: That is the color of Jupiter and Saturn, not Uranus or Neptune.

options.label: White
options.feedback: They are not pure white; the methane gives them a clear blue tint.

options.label: Red-orange
options.feedback: Red-orange is not seen on these planets; it would require different cloud compounds.

items.ok_line: Methane gives Uranus and Neptune their blue-green color.
items.ko_line: Remember methane absorbs red light, leaving blue.
items.exp_text: Both Uranus and Neptune have atmospheres rich in methane, which selectively absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight and scatters the blue and green. This is why they appear as calm, pale blue-green worlds. Uranus tends to look a bit more cyan, while Neptune is deeper blue, partly due to different cloud haze levels.

items.prompt: All four gas giants have a system of what, with many more than the four inner planets?

options.label: Asteroid belts
options.feedback: Asteroid belts lie between Mars and Jupiter, not as part of the gas giants themselves.

options.label: Solid surfaces
options.feedback: Gas giants lack a solid surface, so they do not have surfaces like the inner planets.

options.label: Ring systems
options.feedback: All four do have rings, but the question is about something that far more of them have—moons.

options.label: Moons
options.feedback: Correct. Each gas giant has dozens of moons, with Jupiter and Saturn leading the count, well over the inner planets' few.

items.ok_line: Gas giants have far more moons than rocky planets.
items.ko_line: The common feature is moons, not rings or surfaces.
items.exp_text: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune all possess extensive moon systems, ranging from dozens of small irregular satellites to large round worlds like Ganymede and Titan. These moons likely formed from leftover material in the planets' accretion disks or were captured later. In contrast, the inner rocky planets have only three moons total (Earth's Moon, Mars's two) or none.

items.prompt: For a gas giant like Jupiter, what is the core made of?

options.label: Only hydrogen and helium
options.feedback: The core is not made of the same gas as the rest; it is denser material that is not gas.

options.label: Pure water ice
options.feedback: Ice may be present, but the core also includes rock and metal, not just water ice.

options.label: Rock and metal, possibly with some ice
options.feedback: Correct. The core of a gas giant is a dense mixture of rock, metal, and possibly ice, formed from heavy materials early in the solar system.

options.label: Nothing—the planet is hollow
options.feedback: Gas giants are not hollow; they have a solid core under enormous pressure.

items.ok_line: Jupiter's core is rocky and metallic, not gas.
items.ko_line: The core is heavy, solid material, not hydrogen.
items.exp_text: Deep inside Jupiter, beneath the metallic hydrogen, lies a core made of rock, metal, and potentially ice. This core is believed to be about 10 to 20 times the mass of Earth, though it may be partially dissolved into the surrounding hydrogen. It formed first as the seed that attracted the surrounding gas, and it remains solid or superdense due to extreme pressure.
